v: One January day, a wind warmed Calgary by thirty degrees in four hours.
It's called a chinook. It usually begins with a sudden shift in the wind over the Pacific.
Forced up over the Rockies, the air cools about half a degree for every hundred metres it climbs.
Then it races down the other side, warming about one degree every hundred metres. Warm, dry wind pours onto the prairie.
You can spot it in the sky: a band of cloud parallel to the mountains, with a sharp, straight edge. The chinook arch.
On January eleventh, nineteen eighty-three, Calgary went from minus seventeen to plus thirteen in four hours.

A chinook can even split the map. At seven in the morning on November twenty-second, twenty seventeen, Calgary's airport read minus eight point one. Springbank Airport, just twenty-five kilometres west, read plus eight point four.
An Environment Canada meteorologist put it at about twenty-five chinook days a winter in Calgary. About one every three or four days.
The name comes from the Chinook people of the lower Columbia River, near the Pacific. But it's also known by an Indigenous name: the snow eater.
It melts snow and dries the soil. Trees can start growing too early, and new leaves may be killed by the next frost.

Not everyone loves it. In a study published in two thousand, University of Calgary researchers looked at the diaries of seventy-five migraine patients. For some, migraines were more likely just before a chinook, or on high-wind chinook days. Most weren't affected by either.
A few hours or days later, the cold comes back.
For most people, it's a welcome break from the winter cold.
It's a chinook: a warm, dry wind pouring down the Rockies. An Environment Canada meteorologist puts it at about twenty-five chinook days a Calgary winter.
